title: Mountains Beyond Mountains: The Quest of Dr. Paul Farmer, a Man Who Would Cure the World
author: Tracy Kidder
review:
Once in a generation book, deeply inspiring subject with incredibly engaging narration. I hope reads this book at some point. It is one of the few books I would put up there with Man’s Search for Meaning by Dr. Viktor Frankl as a “every person able to read this owes it to themselves to do so” book. I hesitate to compare anything to Man’s Search for Meaning (and have reserves about this comparison) but both exist in the intersection of incredible people doing something unimaginable and an author able to put that story into beautiful words. ­On top of telling an inspiring story, the author really makes it a page turner. I imagine this would be a really good nonfiction book readers who usually prefer novels.

It’s tempting to just recount the amazing stories from the book, like Paul Farmer literally stealing from the rich at Harvard and smuggling it across borders to the poor in Haiti, but the back of the book will tell you what you need to know. What makes Mountains Beyond Mountains better than just reading Dr. Farmer’s Wikipedia page is Tracy Kidder’s first hand accounts and narration. His interactions with Paul and changing relationship throughout the timeline of the book reveal more than any simple-present tensed article could ever. Seeing the thin cracks in Dr. Farmer’s character thorough Kidder’s eyes, in fact, make him all the more admirable. While Kidder sometimes does start to idolize Farmer in a way that feels dangerously close to the great man theory of history, I think it's clear that he is simply inspired and does not wish to insist Farmer does his work alone or has no flaws. In fact, he makes a point to show how much support Dr. Farmer has at Partners In Health to enable a lot of his activities. That in mind, reading this in a world so full of disrepair, where media feeds refuse to show anything positive, and the thought of being hopeful can come across as naive or even useless - it is wonderful hearing someone so unafraid to have hope. Even if it airs on the side of idealization, maybe we can benefit from being idealistic.

This book serves are a great companion to Bending The Arch, the documentary on Paul Farmer and Partners In Health. If you’re interested by not ready to commit to a book, I’d recommend watching that for free on that Partners In Health website. I’d also recommend you order your copy of Mountains Beyond Mountains as soon as the credits role but I suspect you won’t need my recommendation to do that. Both the documentary and book are powerful and moving. For anyone inspired after reading, I highly recommend supporting Partners in Health by going to pih.org/donate or continuing Paul Farmer’s legacy by joining your local Partner In Health Engage chapter.

title: Fevers, Feuds, and Diamonds: Ebola and the Ravages of History
author: Paul Farmer
review:
If you are interested in the Ebola epidemic from 2013 in Western Africa, this is by far the best single book you can read. Readers interested in just global health, epidemics, Western Africa, or anything similar will also find immense value in this book. It is a case study in how these health crisis happen and a thorough one at that. You cannot begin to understand the epidemic without understanding how the disease spreads. You cannot understand how it spreads without understanding how poverty incubates it. You cannot understand the poverty until you understand the countries. And so on and so forth.

Paul Farmer walks you through his history in the region and with Ebola, discussing not only what is happening on the ground but what he learned about the history of how the region became the way it is. It is very telling that not only did Dr. Farmer decide to include an in depth history of the civil wars that preceded the outbreaks in Sierra Leone and Liberia but that he introduced the section with an admission of shame from his own failing to treat each country with the respect it deserves. A small mix up of the two at 3am clearly haunted him, feeling like he undermined the each country and its history by confusing the two led to a chapters long history lesson. This is the sort of care and compassion Dr. Farmer offers not just to his patients but his readers.

This history lesson is, as readers come to understand, entirely necessary for understanding how pandemics happen. It was not a quiescence that some of the most war torn regions are the ones hit the hardest. And they did not become war torn by sheer luck or purely bad leadership. Plenty of countries have been unlucky and with poor leaders, this was an act done to them and continually maintained. Paul Farmer likes to refer to these systems that perpetuates these conditions structural violence. Through a case study of Ebola in Western Africa, he demonstrates these cycles and takes use along for the ride as a doctor in the middle of it. He also spends time in the modern day, analyzing absurd and often racist practices like the “control over care paradigm.”

Fevers, Feuds, and Diamonds is not just a history lesson. It is first and foremost Paul’s story, he makes it clear that he is only ever able to tell the story he knows. Often this involves quoting or interviewing survivors and witnesses directly, crediting them and their history. Other times it’s Dr. Farmer’s person experiences. He has come close to violent death many times, his personal stories are sometimes shocking. No one, however, is a bigger critic of his work than he is. Much of this book is Paul reflecting and criticizing himself for what he did and did not do. I think it would be hard for any read to not forgive him even if he never asks for it. I hope anyone who considers reading this book does, it’s important to understand our history and to understand the structures still in place causes more “stupid deaths” as Paul Farmer liked to describe them.

title: The Conquest of Bread (Working Classics)
author: Pyotr Kropotkin
review:
This book was much more interesting and easy to read than I expected. I’d recommend it to anyone interested in anarchism, even if only as a passing curiosity. The “18XX” publication date definitely scared me, I was worried it would be dense and largely irrelevant but it was the opposite. I don’t expect anyone to leave the book as a newly found anarcho communist but you might appreciate that perspective more after giving this book some time. It is very much a high level overview missing a lot of detail and not accounting for modern challenges, of course, but that seems to be by design. It is an introduction for a common reader and it does its job well.

The idea of a single kitchen is one of the more surprising and, to me, interesting suggestions. Why, Kropotkin asks, do we have 8 million fires cooking 8 million meals when many of the meals are the same and prepared in the same way at the same time? He suggests have communal kitchens bake the potatoes, distribute them to the home where families can finish them to their taste - or perhaps allow the kitchen to decide how to prepare them -and eat them at their own table with their families. This might go against some of the individualistic ideals many readers grew up with, why should we have to agree to whatever the kitchen decides I eat? I certainly had this feeling when I was reading. There were a lot of these “are you serious?” moments for me throughout the book, some more unreasonable than others. But Kropotkin does a good job of explaining, at a high level, his idea in a reasonable way. I found the text engaging in the way, I often felt challenged but then came to understand the authors intent more.

For the kitchen idea, I started to think about how many people I know still cook all of their meals and how many order prepared meals from fast food or a restaurant. When they don’t order prepared meals, it’s often a simple meal at home for one or two people. To me, this is pretty close to the author’s idea but with a capitalist and liberal spin. We, in fact, do have communal kitchens. They give us options to choose from but we are restricted to their options. Of course, we can go to another restaurant with different options or make something at home. There is a difference but the realistically suggested is less distant than I originally imagine. I can image a government ran DoorDash app that allow families to pick meals from the communal kitchen they wanted while still have some options available at home.

I’m reminded of The People’s Republic of Walmart where authors Leigh Phillips and Michal Rozworski talk about the technological advances that would make a planned economy not only more theoretically possible in a way that would be challenging in the last but also in a way that currently exists but within the private economies of cooperations. A lot of The Conquest of Bread does seem dated and vague but the ideas are still poignant.

Not every chapter of The Conquest of Bread was equally compelling. I found some of the sections, particularly agricultural ones, a little tedious with all the (now) outdated figures and back of the napkin math. Maybe they would have been more compelling if I read it when the book was released but reading it now it did not and the numbers themselves were a lot to keep up with for not much pay off. It did do the job of making the authors point seem well founded but perhaps in an unnecessary way. I’m sure some reading will find these figures to be fascinating but I’m equally sure some readers won’t find other chapters as interesting as I did. I’m sure I would get more out of reading this book multiple times and a deeper understanding of the historical context but as it is, I enjoyed it and it did have an impact on me despite me expecting to only learn about perspectives I disagreed with. I’m not sure I would take it on the beach with me but I would recommend it for anyone interested.

title: The Remedy: Robert Koch, Arthur Conan Doyle, and the Quest to Cure Tuberculosis
author: Thomas Goetz
review:
Well written history of early scientific innovations the lead to the discovery of the cause of Tuberculoses, the world deadliest infectious decease, along with the drama and characters that were apart of that story. Would recommend for anyone interested in early germ theory, the history of science, and TB. All backgrounds will find something fascinating, whether it’s the rise and fall of one of the most influential 19th century scientists, the surprising role of Sherlock Holmes in the history, or the depictions of a time where TB was simply an expected way to die - something shockingly still true in the global south today.

Our main characters are, as the subtitle suggests, Robert Koch, Author Cohen Doyle, and Louis Pasteur. Pasteur is not mentioned in the subtitle but is an important figure, being a consonant in Koch’s life, even after Pasteur’s death. While the story is nonfiction, I still don’t want to spoil their relationship as it has fascinating turns that are thrilling to follow. Cohen Doyle, however, is less involved but still a constant, just one waiting in the wings not so patiently. While I do not believe in the great man theory of history, focusing on these three individual (among other reoccurring characters) creates an interesting and useful narrative device that start in our world before we understood a surgeon should wash their hands or wear globe and ends with germ theory being widely accepted by the scientific community. It is hard to overstate how important of a shift this is in humanity.

While this book is a great telling of early discoveries in TB and germ theory, it is only that. With popular books like Everything is Tuberculosis sitting on tables at the entrances of all western bookstores, it’s worth noting that The Remedy will not catch you up on the history of TB, its effects, or the on going crisis. It is a telling of a curtain place and time in scientific history that has had massive effects on the world. Reading of the aforementioned John Green book will likely enjoy this one as well but I thought it’s worth noting the difference is substance. If it does interest you, though, I absolutely recommend The Remedy. It’s engaging and interesting. I’m unlikely to revisit it anytime soon but still thoroughly enjoyed it.

title: The Black Angels: The Untold Story of the Nurses Who Helped Cure Tuberculosis
author: Maria Smilios
review:
The best telling of this era in tuberculosis with previously untold stories of the nurses who not only cared for the patients at a time there was little hope for recovery but also were critical in the development of treatments we still use today. It’s incredible how Smilios covers both the small scale, individual patients with names and stories being treated by individual nurses with names and stories, and the large scale, how the first drugs were developed and tested changing the course of history. It’s no coincidence, of course, these two scales are the same story. It is rare they are skillfully told at the same time. I hope everyone who considers this book picks it up and gives it the time it deserves.

Smilios does an incredible job at tying all the interweaving stories together and connecting the events of individuals with the events of history. Time is a character as much as any individual is in the book. Unexpected histories tie together from a boxing match that carried the weight of WWII to George Orwell checking into a hospital. They all comeback to Sea View and our nurses. When I fished the book, I flipped back through it and was shocked at all the adventures we went through and how far back the history started.

I went into The Black Angels expecting a personal story from their perspective and it certainly was that. I did not expect it to tell the story of one of the most cortical eras in tuberculosis as well. If The Remedy, a book telling the story about how the bacteria of TB was discovered and early treatment, is the story of the first era in understanding TB, The Black Angels is the start of the era of treating TB but with a more thorough telling. It took me a while to finish this book, in part because how dense it is and how tragic curtain parts are. But it’s an important story that still has a major impact on the world today. TB has been a force of nature for as far back as we have records of anything. This was a pivotal moment in human history, meticulously stitched together into one incredible story. I highly recommend this book for anyone interested in history, global health, hospitals, New York City, or medicine.

title: Politics Is for Power: How to Move Beyond Political Hobbyism, Take Action, and Make Real Change
author: Eitan D. Hersh
review:
Four star book with a five star premise. While it targets college educated, well informed, white, liberals with progressive leanings, it can be useful for those outside of that category. It focused on the concept of “political hobbyism,” engaging in politics through media and online discourse the way one would engage with a hobby, and how different people have moved out of treating it as a hobby and started using politics to enact change. The idea of “politic hobbyism” and breaking out of it was extremely compelling to me even before I read Politics is for Power. I thought about it a lot and decided I might as well actually read the book.

A lot of the earlier part of this book is just examining political hobbyism. I appreciated the story about his dad watching the news before bed and saying “it’s his civic duty.” The author pointed out to his dad the 8 hours already spent listening to the political radio and reading the paper, he admitted he just liked to watch TV before bed and the news was just his pick. I think a lot of us, us being the target demographic of this book, are aware of how much we pay attention to (mostly national) politics simply because we feel compelled to. I thought the author made a very strong case for why we shouldn’t engage in political hobbyism, I think most readers will agree and realize they’ve always agreed but just didn’t pay think much about that habit.

Hersh repeatedly pointed out the way the comfortable life of a well to do, college educated, white person makes them complacent and uninterested in seeking power resulting in political hobbyism. It’s a very compelling argument but the author doesn’t stray too far from that source of hobbyism. Which, in my opinion, is a disservice. Poor minorities also engage with political hobbyism, which could be even more problematic since complacency for already disenfranchised groups could have darker consequences. I don’t think Politics is for Power needed to explore the media landscape and social factors that lead to all forms of hobbyism but the over emphasis on white college educated liberals is painting too narrow of a picture and is potentially harmful. I understand wanting to write a book focusing on that group and their lack of action and appreciate the specific call to action but the narrative he creates might be needlessly simple and narrow.

The constant appeal to “power” is also a little odd and might rub some readers the wrong way. The author explaining how he sometimes feels useless knowing he’s just one vote but then realizes he could persuade others to effectively give him their vote. That is effectively what the book is about, it’s just very blunt. I don’t see this as a draw back, however, it’s understandable not wanting to sugar coat what the “power” required for chance entails. I just wanted to mention that since it did stand out to me, along with some other minor points I haven’t mentioned, and does affect the tone of the book. I still highly recommend it, if the message speaks to you, it’s important that you act on it.

title: The People’s Republic of Walmart: How the World’s Biggest Corporations are Laying the Foundation for Socialism
author: Leigh Phillips
review:
One of the best explanations of planned economies, would recommend for anyone interested in the tonic. Even if you’re confident in its ineffectiveness or impracticality, I think you’ll find The People’s Republic of Walmart very interesting and will come out of it with a fuller picture of the topic.

This book is pretty short and pretty pointed. With all book like that I find myself half glad it can serve as an accessible point of entry and half annoyed it didn’t go deeper into any of the topics despite the room to do so. The People’s Republic of Walmart does a good job at balancing these two. For the most part, it did a good job at giving an high level view of a topic without glaring omissions. The only outlier in that is the author’s insistence on the role of democracy in the planned economy. They regularly asserted that democracy was foundational to a functioning planned economy throughout the book but I never heard the full explication as to why. This felt like it could have been an additional chapter but instead it was largely glossed over.

I expected this book to be more about deep diving into the planned economy of Walmart but the title mostly points to one of the central idea of the book, only diving into that topic directly for a few chapters. I was happy to have the broader scope, however, and think they made a strong case for the topic as a whole. Although I now want a longer book that focuses just on the logistics of large firms and their comparability to national economies. I enjoyed the book though, probably won’t revisit it any time soon, but loved reading it. Maybe grab the audio book for a long road trip.

title: Blackshirts and Reds: Rational Fascism and the Overthrow of Communism
author: Michael Parenti
review:
If you’re interested in a Marxist analysis of fascism, the history of communism, and the role of the west in demonizing communism from the perspective of a defender of existing socialism, this is a great read. I have to specify the last part mostly because I understand many readers would be upset by Parenti’s defense of the USSR. While a lot of the west has been pushing anti-USSR propaganda, notably information from the Black Book of Communism, Parenti goes what I consider too far in the opposite direction and suggests the Soviet Union was, in fact, a successful experiment. Siting that even those that live in former Soviet countries believe life was better under communism. If you, like me, have talked to those residents, you might realize this isn’t a popular sentiment.

That said, the fact that I disagree with the author does not mean I should avoid him. In fact, I should seek out a better understanding of the roots of our disagreement, giving me all the more reason to read his works. Additionally, I don’t want to overshadow the rest of this book with the few chapters defending Stalin. The earlier sections on fascism were fascinating and quite the page turner. I was deeply engaged with this book through its entirety. Parenti is no stranger to speaking directly to his audience and it shows in his writing. While I do recommend reviewing his resources actionable and researching topics he discusses yourself, I do still recommend this book.

title: The Cultural Revolution: A People's History, 1962-1976
author: Frank Dikötter
review: Great read, I don’t read much history but this book was captivating. It’s a sometimes hard to believe history of an important era western schools tend to gloss over. The writing style makes it feel like a novel which I could see being a little polarizing for readers. I enjoyed it but I might wait awhile to go back and read the other two books in the series. The author did a great job of working in citations to the narrative style without messing up the flow. This might be a personal problem most readers don’t share but I did find keeping track of all the unanglicized names. Names are used often to add to the immersive style but I often felt it would have been easier to follow if it read like a more traditional nonfiction work. This could be normal for books in this genre but it was new to me. Still enjoyable and would recommend.

title: The Great Transformation: The Beginning of Our Religious Traditions
author: Karen Armstrong
review:
Wonderful read, very informative, engaging narrative, and very appreciated perspective. Highly recommend for anyone interested in world religions. If you are religious it might help you appreciate your own religion, if you are non-religious it might help you appreciate the incredible technology of religion we’ve developed as a species. If you’re a non-religious person but appreciate the wisdom of the Greek philosophers, that is also covered and ties together with the rest of the “axial age.”

The idea of an “axial age” being an error where all of the world’s major modern religions and schools of thought developed is interesting, as if religion and philosophy was a stage of evolution we were going towards eventually. This age spans many centuries so it might be a stretch to stay it was around the same time. Religions did exist before the axial age, touched on some early in the book, so it could a number of other factors that led to these religions sticking around. That said, it does provide a great narrative for the story of these movements. The author connects theme and speculates on the pressures that created each one.

This book does treat religion primary as a philosophy and social movement which is appropriate while discussing their early development. I think that’s important to note, though, for readers. If you want to learn about the rich cultural history of various religions, this might not be the book for that but you might still enjoy it. It’s very respectful of the subject and very thorough in its history.

title: How Europe Underdeveloped Africa
author: Walter Rodney
review:
This is one of the rare, unambiguously, five star books. It is a history book that takes on a monumental story of the active underdevelopment of African countries and communities by Europe and the United States. To discuss this history, Dr. Rodney has to first provide the historical context of Africa that many western readers were never taught. Considering how large Africa is, this is no small task but the author pulls it off well and with engaging prose. I’m sure there was more information left out than included, I would have loved to have read an unabridged series on the same topic from Dr. Rodney.

As the afterwards points out, one of the amazing aspects of How Europe Underdeveloped Africa is that it is directed at the people of the world, not the leaders. There is a sense of mischief in reading it, as if it’s a history you were not meant to hear. Regardless of the intentionality of this history being omitted from textbooks, it is a critical history that every person sharing this planet should be aware of. I went in with a vague sense of western exploitation but did not understand its execution or depth. Everyone owes it to themselves to add this book to their reading list. It’s enjoyable, informative, and likely to have a profound effect on your understanding of the world.

title: Capitalist Realism: Is There No Alternative?
author: Mark Fisher
review:
Thought provoking and unique read, highly recommend but it might not be for everyone. It is pretty short, though, so might as well give it a try. I flipped between hating this book and loving it multiple times but ended on loving it. With pop culture references from Kafka to Goodfellas, it has aged very well despite how quickly culture moves now and it continues to be insightful. Some of the topics Fisher covered have really stuck with me and change my view on some aspects of our world. I appreciate his description of his university students skipping class to play video games and enjoy fast food as being in a state of “soft narcosis.” I also appreciate the forward and afterward of my copy providing important context for this book. If you do read it, be sure to give those the attention they deserve.

The writing style might be the most decisive part of this book. For example, I didn’t quite understand how literal some of Fisher’s comparisons were ment to be. He made a strong case for late capitalism leading to the rise of depression and even dyslexia but he lost me when he schizophrenia is the “out edge of capitalism”, bi-polar “interior of capitalism”, and that capitalism itself is bi-polar with its boom and bust cycles. I don’t fully understand what that means, I understand the comparison of boom-bust and manic-depression but is the implication that this causes the disorder? That seems like such a stretch that trying in trying to justify it, I feel like I’m missing the point. Which, of course, I could be.

Many parts I had to reread either because of the wording or the way he describes his abstract ideas. This is probably just as reflective of me as it is the author though. Even the title and central concept, “capitalist realism” was confusing to me. To me, even after reading, the phrase sounds like it should be describing a reflection that is going to take place in the book, equivalent to “being realistic about capitalism.” but, as I understand it, it is really mean as the name of a philosophy akin to “postmodernism” or “existentialism”. It might sound like a small grammatical difference but its use as a school of thought makes a lot of the grammar jarring.

This, along with the previous example, illustrates the strangeness of this book. I hope that i intrigues you more than it worries you, however. It made for a unique experience that was enjoyable. I highly recommend this Capitalist Realism, it’s a one of one experience that I think most people will benefit from reading.

title: Thoughts Without A Thinker: Psychotherapy From A Buddhist Perspective
author: Mark Epstein
review:
I enjoyed this book and would recommend it to readers of Mark Epstein but if you haven’t read his other books, I would direct you there first. Thoughts Without a Think is Epstein’s first book and it does show some. I don’t think he had fully found his voice yet, it is written very academically and can come off as very dry and distant because of that.

For example, Epstein wrote in the last chapter “When Freud wrote about the oceanic feeling as the apotheosis of the mystical feeling and when Fromm extolled wellbeing as the fruition of Buddhist meditation, they were overlooking a simple but essential point: meditation is not just about creating states of well-being; it is about destroying the belief in an inherently existent self.” To me, this writing just comes off as technical and dense. If you enjoy that writing style you’ll probably love this book but it’s not what I’ve come to expect from reading the authors more recent works.

One of my favorite parts of this book, however, is how deeply Epstein dives into Buddhist traditions and mythology. His more recent releases shies away from that to an extent or, at the very least, it is rarely a focus. I feel like I learned more about Buddhism as a tradition with a rich history from this book than I have from other meditation-focused “secular Buddhist” books.

title: Abundance
author: Ezra Klein
review:
Enjoyable and interesting read but left me feeling I was never given what I was promised. I left with some interesting ideas, some information on policy history, and a vague idea of needed change. I would recommend this book but no need to rush out and put it on the top of your read list.

The authors noted that they thought about calling this book “The Abundance Agenda” but decided to move away from the “agenda” approach. That’s a great explanation of what I didn’t like about the book. With some speculation from my end, it sounds like Abundances started as a book about an agenda, planning on giving a list of policy changes. Later on, it moved into an ideology focused book. In doing so, it never finished the policy agenda but and never fully fleshed out the ideology. I’m definitely filling in a lot of gaps but I think it illustrates my feeling on the book even if it’s not accurate. The authors spend the majority of the book describing failed policy with vague ideas of a solution. While I appreciate the need for more of “the science of science”, I also wanted more of an explanation of what that looks like. Perhaps they were trying too hard to make the book accessible and short to find a wider audience, which is understandable. Unfortunately, I think it suffers too much from its brevity. Maybe they could have split it into multiple books, recommended further reading along the way, or release an unabridged version.

Later in the book, while debunking the myth of “genius inventors” changing history instead promoting the idea that inventions tend to be a slow communal process, the authors used Thomas Edison as an example. They disproved the genius inventor theory by pointing out that the lightbulb is just an iteration of the safety lamp created by a different genius inventor, Humphrey Davy. I understand the point is that it wasn’t Edison alone but why just pin it on a different figure with a similar “genius inventor” mythos? That was an easy opportunity to use the language they hope that readers adopt. Something as simple as “in the 19th century Royal Institution worked with coal miners and built on yet more known technologies to develop early safety lamps.” Maybe include “(often attributed to the individual Humphrey Davy)” at the end to hammer the point home. It’s small things like this that made me feel like the authors weren’t committed to conveying a specific message through out the book.

Towards the end, the authors mentioned wanting Abundance to convey a “lens” to see policy and change through. An ideology, not a to-do list. It’s certainly important to have real examples to demonstrate your philosophy but, for me, the book’s focus on bad policy but insistence to not suggest specific fixes was not a good explanation of their philosophy. If this book was purely historical from an impartial narrator, I would be more content with little actionable items (actionable not just being policy suggestions but *how* to apply the lens they suggest). Given the more involved and activist nature, however, it feels like an argument they never finished. Three stars is still a positive review and I do recommend this book if you’re interested. There were small history lessons and ideas, like the “bottleneck detective”, that I really enjoyed. It’s short so not too much of an investment but maybe wait for the paperback or a second hand copy. I do hope their ideology is widely adopted and I look forward to future books where the authors expand on the ideas of Abundance.

title: The Zen of Therapy: Uncovering a Hidden Kindness in Life
author: Mark Epstein
review:
Would recommend for those looking for a look inside various talk therapy session and the lessons the therapist is trying to convey without saying it - all supported with memorable poems and stories from the Zen practice of Buddhism. You don’t need to be in therapy, be Buddhist, or know much about Buddhism, to enjoy this book. You’ll learn a lot on Mark Epstein’s perspective on his work and how it’s affected his life.

I actually first read this book when it came out but remembered not enjoying it and forcing myself to finish it. I recently finished Going On Being and wanted to give this one another try. To my surprise, I really enjoyed it this time around. Mark Epstein books often feel similar and this book’s four seasons structure didn’t do much for me. The second time around, though, the emphasis on talk therapy and Zen Buddhist traditions stood out. I liked the collection of slices of the patients life and how the author related them to lessons he’s learned from his own practice and research.

Of course, it is a Mark Epstein book so expect an emphasis on Freud and D. W. Winnicott. I do enjoy it but it does occasionally feel like a narrow view. He does acknowledge their shortcomings, though, while still taking what lessons still exist in their work. I do think the author tries to avoid this but some of his writing occasionally sounds a little too “new age spiritual” for lack of a better term. I mean to say, vague feelings that insist they are profound (not to say they aren’t and not to say he is insisting, that’s just the vibe) than some western readers might relate too. That could just as well be a reflection of my personal self conscious feelings than of the author’s writing though. Either way don’t let that scare you away but don’t be surprised when he sounds profoundly touched by the lyrics of “Row, Row, Row, Your Boat.”

title: Going on Being: Buddhism and the Way of Change
author: Mark Epstein
review:
For readers that enjoyed Dan Harris’s 10% Happier but thought “let’s not beat around the bush - tell me the religious teaching along with the psychological.” It’s of my favorite reads from Mark Epstein. It’s a self reflective story of his early experience in developing his Buddhist practice while he was also studying and in the early stages of becoming a psychotherapist. It has all the hallmarks of Epstein’s work with references to D. W. Winnicott, Freud, and his Buddhist masters. With stories from his trainings by world famous teachers from Ram Dass to Joseph Goldstein, he seamlessly connects deep and profound Buddhist lessons to theories of mind and psychoanalysis that make the lessons more poignant. I appreciate the narrative structure of a loose autobiography. It never insists you care about the authors story, only what he learned, but most readers will care anyway.

As much as I enjoy Mark Epstein’s works, a lot of his books feel very similar - some borderline interchangeable. Luckily, I love that book he keeps writing and enjoy the new flavors of each release. I love hearing his stories from his Buddhists practice combined with his readings in psychoanalysis. Those are lessons I often need to hear more than once so I’m more the grateful for each new opportunity to read similar stories. Going On Being, however, stands out from the line up. Perhaps it felt more personal, the narrative structure felt compelling in a unique way, the core concept resonates with me, or maybe it just said what I needed to hear when I needed to hear it. Regardless, it is one of my favorite books Mark Epstein has written. It the perfect starting point for his works and if you’ve read a couple of books by him and didn’t quite love it, this might be the one to change your mind.

title: Lives of the Stoics: The Art of Living from Zeno to Marcus Aurelius
author: Ryan Holiday
review:
Good overview of the major stoics, although I don’t know them well myself so if there were any glaring omissions I wouldn’t have noticed. It’s exactly what the back of the books says, if you want to learn about famous stoics it will get the job done. I was hoping for something that told a more cohesive story throughout. Something closer to At the Existentialist Cafe by Sarah Bakewell. Instead, the books reads like a series of unconnected biographies with occasional references to each other. If that’s what you want, it’ll be a great but wasn’t exactly what I was hoping for.

I can see how this book would be a great companion to other stoic studies instead of a one off, as it was for me. If you’re already deep into it and want to fill in the gaps and have a references for when a name comes up you don’t quite remember, it would be well suited to that because of its disconnected nature. I didn’t love that and ended up butting the book down for a while before finishing it because of that but it could be a plus for other readers.

title: The Divide: A Brief Guide to Global Inequality and its Solutions
author: Jason Hickel
review:
Well written and easy read that introduces a lot of history and concepts important for understanding the unjust world we live in, how we got here, and where we’re headed. I highly recommend The Divide, I’m not sure it’s possible to have a well constructed understanding of our place in the world without understanding the topics Hickel discusses and I appreciated the recommendations and solutions towards the end of the book. The contents can be depressing and upsetting but he never slips into nihilism.

The one star missing, which I might change after I’ve spent more time with reflecting on The Divide, is largely due to how high level a lot of the discussions were, a lack of further reading suggestion to make up for the very introductory nature, and, to a lesser extent, a lack of specific calls to action for the reader to do. I’m very sympathetic to the fact that this book is sold at Barnes and Noble and needs a general audience to buy it but it is already a quick read, more details could have make stronger arguments. Note, I did read the audiobook so maybe there were footnotes that covered more ground that I missed out on. But 4 stars is still a glowing review and I hope everyone who comes across this book gives it the time it deserves.

Side Note for Audible Readers: while Jonathan Cowley’s performance was great, for some reason it was mixed to be extremely bass heavy. You have to use your phone’s built in equalizer to make it listenable and even then I’d suggest not listen to it in a car.

title: Everything Is Tuberculosis: The History and Persistence of Our Deadliest Infection
author: John  Green
review:
Great overview of the history of TB, our role in its continuous destruction, the author’s relationship to it, and the story of a wonderful young man who fought through it despite everything seemingly stacking up against him. It also doubles as a great introduction into global health in general, it uses TB as a case study to analyze the inequity we have created through centuries of exploitation and unfair practices. It’s also a very enjoyable and somewhat short read so I hope people who would be interested in improving global health given the opportunity but have not had a good introduction pick this one up. Ideal for someone who has little knowledge or TB but would enjoy learning about it, they might not realize just how unjust our social order, as Green likes to describe it, is for people in the global south.

Don’t let the author scare you away, yes it is that John Green from The Fault in Our Stars but he has since become one of the most vocal anti-Tuberculosis activists - helping large charity events, aiding in pressuring pharmaceutical companies to lower costs, speaking at the United Nations (if you look up “John Green UN Speech” you’ll find a great sample of what this book is about), and so on. He was humble in his writing, often referring to “activist” online making changes while leaving out his role in it.

I do, regrettably, only give 4 stars only because the book The Phantom Plague by Vidya Krishnan exists. If I had read that I would have given this book 5 stars, maybe I’ll reflect and change my mind in the future. That book is very similar but I found the random stories about TB more compelling and the social analysis to be more thorough and direct. Both things this book could have benefited from, although it would have risked sounding too much like Krishnan’s book. I still loved the story of Henry Reider sprinkled throughout the story and found this book more approachable for a general audience less invested in TB and global health. All things considered, it’s good that both exist and it’s a good use of the “John Green” name recognition that’s likely to get more people to pick it up. I still highly recommend this book, just also pick up a copy of The Phantom Plague while you’re at the book store.

title: Untangled: Walking the Eightfold Path to Clarity, Courage, and Compassion
author: Koshin Paley Ellison
review: Enjoyable read from the perspective of a zen teacher who grew up in the United States. A lot of emphasis on aspects of life as being “a place of practice” with a description and example of what that means. I do think this is very much targeted at western people who are not buddhist, such as myself, since it gives advice from the dharma but doesn’t actually bring up any religious aspect of the Buddha’s teachings. It is an easy read and pleasant, personally not too much stood out to me that I’ll keep with me. If you just like having these sort of books in rotation I would suggest it but if you only want to dip your toes in maybe there are better options.

title: New York, New York, New York: Four Decades of Success, Excess, and Transformation
author: Thomas Dyja
review: Great overview on the modern history of NYC. The author had the insurmountable task of summarizing a complicated history of a city with a population comparable to many influential countries. He managed to touch on geographic, political, and cultural history in an easy to follow and compelling narrative. Very useful for context to jump off a deeper understanding of aspects of NYC.

title: In the Buddha's Words: An Anthology of Discourses from the Pali Canon (The Teachings of the Buddha)
author: Venerable Bhikkhu Bodhi
review:
Interesting and insightful translation with supporting commentary for historical context and clarity. Do keep in mind that the Pali Canon is a religious text so it is not necessarily written for modern audiences’ entertainment. I suggest reading it as a historical and cultural piece. Many people find the repetition and format of the translated text to be tedious, I personally thought it was as amusing in its absurdity at times and poetic at others.

I would highly recommend everyone read In The Buddha’s Word but would encourage them to jump around if they feel so inclined. Just reading the introductions to each section would probably be a more entertaining experience, maybe dive into the sutras themselves when an introduction catches your attention. It is a long book but I enjoy having it as a daily ritual, the repetition (which the translator already cut back on for western audiences) was calming as I made my morning coffee.

I am unlikely to read it in its entirety again but might find other translations with similar contextual summaries to further my understanding of the religion and its history.

title: Metamorphoses: In Search of Franz Kafka
author: Karolina Watroba
review:
Wonderfully written journey through Kafka’s life and the authors relationship with it and its history. You will learn a lot about Franz Kafka from multiple perspectives, not just the man but the idea of “Kafka.” I knew about his life, the classic story of the depressed author from Prague, but I didn’t know just how misleading that story is and how important the story of “the classic story of the depressed author from Prague” is to understanding the man.

I went in hoping to learn more about Franz Kafka’s life and came out with that knowledge and so much more critical context and history. This book also is my absolute favorite genre: non-fiction that’s as much about the author as it is the thing in the title. It is nice to try to separate yourself from your writing but it’s an impossible task so you might as well lean into it and give the reader more clarity on your perspective. Plus, you get a narrative and story to follow outside of the subject.

title: The Phantom Plague: How Tuberculosis Shaped History
author: Vidya Krishnan
review:
I keep coming back to this book, the story of Tuberculosis is fascinating and haunting. The way Vidya Krishnan compiles and presents the narrative makes for an incredible read that sparks feelings fascination, horror, and hope. The horror, however, does not simply come from the infectious disease. As Krishnan details, tuberculosis was once a terror of nature’s design but since its cure it has become a terror of our own design. Slipping into cracks in our social order we pretend don’t exist.

The Phantom Plague is more than a history of the world deadliest infection disease. That story, driven by Vidya Krishnan’s writing and analysis, is also the history of anti-bacterial disinfectants, vampires, heartfelt individual stories, and failures in our society. Don’t read this book to learn only about Tuberculosis, read it to learn about our shared world and the complexities of it that lead to wonderful connections and deadly inequity.

I read this book a while ago and just never wrote a review here. I was worried I wouldn’t have much to say but it has really stuck with me. Since I’ve read The Phantom Plague, two high profile TB books have been released in Black Angels and Everything Is Tuberculosis (finished them now, both recommended though) and this one still stands out as the best high level discussion. It connects anecdote with large scale events, does not shy away from criticizing flaws in the heart of global inequality, and discusses the history of colonialism and capitalist experiments that create and perpetuate the problems we’ve designed. I recommend this book as highly as I can recommend anything.

title: Based on a True Story: A Memoir
author: Norm Macdonald
review: Take everything you know about memoirs and through it out the window. Now let me tell you about a little thing Norm MacDonald made - a memoir. Allow me to rephrase that - not a memoir. Some of the stories from Norm were shocking, others unbelievable, and many both. I don't know if I've lost respect for norm for some of the things he's done or if I've gained respect for his courage to tell it. However, I wonder how much of this book Norm (MacDonald) wrote at all. There are a few sections in particular that clue me into this, less thoughtful readers might miss these clues entirely. The only way to find out it to read it for yourself. I don't think I can recommend that, however, on account of the horrific things norm admits to and the questionable quality of his character. Nah, he's a good man but for real don't read this book unless you want to. Four stars because that answering machine bit killed me.

title: The Disordered Cosmos: A Journey into Dark Matter, Spacetime, and Dreams Deferred
author: Chanda Prescod-Weinstein
review:
Must read for anyone going into or interested in any of the sciences. Realistically, I think everyone should read this but I say that about a lot of books so I narrowed it down some. This book revolves around the cosmos and people. Dr. Prescod-Weinstein explains aspects of the cosmos she is fascinated by in an easy to understand manner and then uses those as anchor points to explore the human side of science. Imagine if you replaced the glorified stories of famous scientists in Cosmos by Carol Sagan with the raw experiences of everyday scientists working right now. The Disordered Cosmos teaches you as much about the process of science as the science itself, which is rarely covered in these type of books.

I was surprised how much this book focused on the social and systemic issues in science but it was a very welcome surprise. In fact, I was happy to have that surprise as I don't think I would have bought the book if it's title was more explicit about what it covers. That's not to say the title is misleading - we are the cosmos and it is us that creates our understanding of it. We are the discorded cosmos. In that way, The Disordered Cosmos covers the cosmos more fully than any books I’ve ever read. Our theories and models do not exist outside of ourselves, most books leave “us” out of the picture while describing what we know. While the interpersonal and systemic issues this books discusses focus on Dr. Prescod-Weinstein's area of study, the lessons learned can be applied more generally to just about anything. I highly recommend everyone reads this book and they share their copy with their friends.

title: Kafka in 90 Minutes (Great Writers in 90 Minutes Series)
author: Paul Strathern
review:
I’ve read a few of this ___ in 90 minutes books and this one may be my least favorite. I certainly enjoyed it and thought it had a well written and concise story of Kafka’s life but found some choices a little surprising. Given that Kafka exclusively wrote fiction (outside of his journals and letters), I would expect more careful selection of words around the plots. While spoiling a Kafka book hardly ruins it (you haven’t read one of his books until you‘ve read it more than once) but it certainly dulls the excitement of the first read. This book went through the entire plot of The Trial and The Metamorphosis is some detail, explaining away every twist and turn new reader might have enjoyed experiencing first hand. A books like “Kafka in 90 Minutes” presents itself as a good place to start with the author so spoiling two of his most popular works doesn’t seem thoughtful.

Worst of all, I didn’t find either of these stories’ summary to be necessary. I don’t know if the author decides you can’t have an introduction to Kafka if you don’t know the plot of a couple of his works but I found no real reason for either. The summary of The Trial took up a significant amount of the book, which I should remind you is marketed on how concise it is. Furthermore, and a very nit picky note, the author explained a the end of The Trial’s parable incorrectly. It was a minor mistake that a slip of the tongue could explain but it changes the possible meaning of the parable. Kafka even explored the importance of this nuance in The Trial itself - how this mistake slipped past the author and editors is beyond me, especially considering the end of this book quotes the parable in it entirety (which, at the very least, did save me a trip to my bookshelf to confirm the author made a mistake).

With that all said, the book still does it’s job and wouldn’t try to prevent anyone from picking it up. Just be sure to read The Trial and The Metamorphosis first if you want to go into those stories blind.

title: The Metamorphosis
author: Franz Kafka
review:
Bizarre story that captures the human experience precisely in its stubborn avoidance of its own absurdity.

Given its modest length this short story should be on everyone’s reading list. The plot is well paced and rhythmically provides developments at the peak of the reader’s anxiety never not a page more. I found the book to be a hit autobiographical, giving some insight into the dark view Kafka has of himself and his relationships. I hope this story continues to be a classic for years to come.

title: The Trial
author: Franz Kafka
review:
I didn’t find the book exceptional at first but the following week after I read it my mind kept wondering back. The text is very straightforward, almost dry, in a way that’s deceptive. The experience of reading the book feels like a confusing but simple trip to the bank. You understand what’s going on, at least enough to keep up, but you never understand the full picture. After putting the book down, it becomes more like waking up from a dream about going to the bank. Nothing makes sense but you were so convinced it was sensible enough in the moment. That’s not to say the book is nonsense, in fact, it’s incredibly written. It’s the first work of fiction I’ve discovered that truly replicated a literal nightmare. While Lovecraft might be more “nightmarish,” I rarely have dreams of universal monstrosities. My nightmares are just nonessential enough to make me feel trapped but realistic enough to make me believe them. That is the experience The Trial offers.

It’s hard to pinpoint what the book is likely about. As such, it’s ripe for projection. There are a dozen different ideas you’ll find fit nicely into the story but none are obviously what Kafka was going for. That might be frustrating at time but it allows you to think about the book for hours trying to decipher a meaning. For similar reasons, this book also rewards multiple readings considerably. Givens it’s modest length and easy reading, there’s no reason not to give it a few goes.

I wish I could better express the haunting and reliable feelings this book has offers me, hopefully I’ll update this review in the future. For now, I’d highly recommend it to anyone interested in a classic that uniquely captures the emotions of waking up from a nightmare.

title: Science Fictions
author: Stuart Ritchie
review:
Great disambiguation of the practical way science is done in academia. “Science” has become a bit of a big work in recent years that isn’t always specific. This books dives into the mechanics of research and publication in a very non-ambiguous way that demystifies the field. That said, it’s not about that specifically, it’s just a nice side effect. The book is about how researchers can publish misleading, bad, or out right fraudulent papers that can skew the public’s and even other scientists’ understanding of something.

Despite how hot of a topic this could be, the author doesn’t treat it as such. Instead he is very direct and to the point about what is going on and how to change it. As he says in the introduction, there are some areas of interest that are outright pseudosciences such as astrology or creationism. He has little interest in these areas in the context of this book. It is concerned first and foremost with the implementation of science; research. He discusses popular studies and books that mislead the public (some of which you have surely read), how research and be misleading, and how to prevent it in the future.

The writing itself is also well executed, it is easy to read and free of any dense language that could have easily slipped into a book like this. I highly recommend it for anyone who want to understand science and the state of science in a fuller way.

title: The Trauma of Everyday Life
author: Mark Epstein
review:
I didn’t find much to take issue with but I was not captured the same was I was by Going To Pieces or Advice Not Given. From what I can tell, Epstein’s books are mostly similar - a combination of lessons from psychotherapy and Buddhism. That is exactly what this book is so I suppose I got what I wanted from it. Yet, I don’t feel as inspired by it as the two books I mentioned. It’s possible that has more to do with me than the book but I suspect I won’t be the only reader with this take. As much as I love the bits and pieces from both perspectives Epstein offers, I also feel the need for a clearer structured. Advice Not Given followed the four noble truths and Going To Pieces follows the eightfold path. This book had a much looser structure and I can only guess that is the reason it didn’t land for me quite as well. I also found the frequent references to the same couple of psychotherapists a little worrisome. That’s a pretty easy way to fall victim to poor analysis. Putting too much emphasis on a single persons research and thoughts means if they fall into question then so does every point you made in reference to them. Why Buddhism is True had a similar problem, it relied on evolutionary psychology which upon further investigation is more of a pseudoscience than a science, bringing the entire book into question. I don’t know Epstein’s references have any reason for suspicion but the constant reference made me feel wary.

With that said, the book was still quite enjoyable and I’d recommend to anyone whose already read the two previously mention books by the same author. It scratches that buddhist itch some of us have and is very easy to read. I have the other two books four stars and found this one clearly a notch below them so I naturally had to go with three. Don’t let that dissuade you, however, if your considering picking this one up then I say go for it.

title: Digital Minimalism: Choosing a Focused Life in a Noisy World
author: Cal Newport
review:
Insightful but, at times, insufferable. This book as a lot going for it. The text is very easy to read and pretty engaging. Newport mixing in many anecdotes that help make his point but also gives the reader a quick and fun narrative to follow. This has a nice side effect of making these short examples very memorable. I also appreciated how actionable a lot of the advice was. You aren't just told about the problems with over-engagement with digital devices and to make changes, you're given a clear guide on what specifically you should change and where to start. If you're someone who thinks that you use your smartphone a bit to much but not sure if you want to do anything about it, this will argue why you should make a change and how to do it.

However... as much as I want to love this book and as glad as I am that it exists, I can't recommend it to most people. The kind of person who would read an entire book called "Digital Minimalism" probably isn't the same person unconvinced that there constant smart phone indulgences isn't a problem. Many readers, myself included, will read this book nodding their head and saying "that *is* good advice." While I did pick up a thing or two from this book, I mostly just reinforced beliefs I already had. Despite already being on Newport's "team," I found most of his arguments unsatisfying. He often mentions stories of people who were happier because of their appreciation for things digital devices make us avoid but rarely did he present a well formed argument. Most of his justification was something to the effect of "you'll be happier with less digital devices because that is what makes people happier." To his credit, there were a few studies referenced but they hardly carried the book.

Worst of all, and I really hate to say it, is how coy and mug Newport sometimes came across. In a book about everyone else being wrong, you might expect an author to carefully present their case to not come across as too smug but I'm not convinced Newport made such an attempt. I will save you from examples but it really made the book less enjoyable. I, of course, am not claiming this is a reflection of Newport as a person, it's just an unfortunate aspect of this book I could have done without. I understand it can be tough to write a book like this without sounding smug at any point but it's definitely possible. Hivemind by Sarah Rose Cavanagh, for example, covers a lot of similar ideas but never once comes across as smug. In fact, just go read that book instead, it's really good.

I don't know if I would recommend this book as a serious read but, being so short and easy to read, I don't mind recommend it as a quick dose of inspiration for when you're digital habits of been gone unchecked for too long.

title: Standing at the Edge: Finding Freedom Where Fear and Courage Meet
author: Joan Halifax
review:
As enjoyable and inspiring as some of the passages in this book may be, I always felt the author never exploring anything with much depth. It suffered from what a lot of Buddhist modernist books suffer from: in an attempt to be scientific and Buddhist, it’s not quite scientific and not quite Buddhist. Luckily, this book doesn’t lean on that relationship as much as a book like Why Buddhism Is True so it’s not a major hindrance. Most of the book is anecdotes, stories, and lessons learned from the authors life.

What you’re left with is some nice and surprisingly wholesome stories (despite how dark many of them are) and some lessons from a Buddhist monk. Only a few of the lessons really stuck with me, most I felt required more explanation that was never given. If you’re, like me, just looking for some surface layer and easily digestible Buddhist nonfiction then this book will serve you well. Otherwise, I’m not sure who I would recommend it to.

title: Hivemind: The New Science of Tribalism in Our Divided World
author: Sarah Rose Cavanagh
review:
Going into this book, I assumed it would be a condemning of groups of people who think in a hive mind. At the time, I didn’t even realize how presumptuous or pessimistic that thought was. Instead, I was delighted an optimist and fair objective dissection of the oh-so-human practice of thinking in a hive mind. As I came to realize, “hive mind” is not the dirty term that describes a thing we should be fighting an shameful of, it is simply a the way humans function. Hivemind dives into the interconnectedness of thoughts and the impact that has on the world. Sure, there is plenty to worry about but it is not a thing to worry about in itself.

The author covers this topic in a shockingly positive way and in a very engaging writing style. While it might seem formulaic to some readers, I found the structure of the book and it’s paragraphs incredibly entertaining. The brief chapter introductions of descriptive writing breaks up the text and sets a new tone. The way chapters act as a vehicle to summarize interviews was fun and effective. Despite it’s scary sounding premise, I would highly recommend this book to everyone, especially as a light summer read to take on the beach.

title: Behave: The Biology of Humans at Our Best and Worst
author: Robert M. Sapolsky
review:
Despite this books length I was pretty upset when it ended. Behave is an enjoyable read with plenty of personality that provides a wide introduction to behavioral psychology. Don't let the page count turn you off, it is an easy read and a fun one at that. The author is not afraid to inject himself into the book, I really enjoyed all of the anecdotes and quips. Additionally, the content itself is broken up into relatively short chapters and those chapters are broken up into subheadings. If you're not interested in learning about one of the topics, it's pretty easy to skip right past. In fact, at one point he basically says that the next section will be awfully boring and isn't critical to understanding anything else, basically suggesting you skip it.

If the synopsis interests you then you should absolutely pick up this book. Human behavior is so bizarre and the ways we learn about it are equally strange. The best comparison for this book I can think of is Thinking, Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahneman. Imagine that book if it was about human behavior instead of human thought. This is one of the few books that I genuinely think I will be revisiting in the next year.

title: The Anthropocene Reviewed: Essays on a Human-Centered Planet
author: John  Green
review:
There are few projects that have moved me to the point of tears so regularly and have inspired my own creatively so deeply. I don’t know how to reconcile the fact that other people will read this book as it means so much to me. John Greens recount of his human experience is engaging and memorable, they don’t outstay their welcome and don’t let you forget about them.

The overall review format is a wonderful tool for generating essay prompts that lead to deeper insights into the life of the author and the human experience. Additionally, the make the book easy to make your own: Jumping from essay to essay as you please is just as valid of a reading experience as reading cover to cover. No essay is dependent on a previous so you are not penalized for skipping about.

I highly recommend everyone give this book a try. If you’re not sure, there are easy ways to sample the book before you buy it seeing as it’s a collection of short stories. You could go to your local book store and just read a random essay, go to your favorite podcast app and listen to an episode of The Anthropocene Reviewed, or go to YouTube and watch one of the essay videos on the VlogBrothers channel (Auld Lang Syne is a good one to start with).

title: Why I Am Not a Buddhist
author: Evan Thompson
review:
Essential read for anyone interested in the western Buddhist movement - be it a personal, cultural, or academic interest. It very clearly and concisely explains problem with “Buddhist modernism” that the author finds troublesome. This movement is something many reader in America and Europe are very quickly buying into, myself included. It is in good humor and at no points attacks the people who are contributing to this movement. In fact, he often commends the people associated with it but just points out parts of their thinking he find unjustified.

The writing in Why I Am Not A Buddhist is, on the whole, very simple and easy to read. Some academic works like this one can be dense - I’ll sometimes decide to move from a comfy chair to a desk to read some. This one, however, is quite a present read. Aside from a couple of chapters, it required minimum effort to follow and was even exciting. Hearing him name drop the heavy hitters in the Buddhist modernist world was exciting; he would introduce an idea of their (very thoroughly I might add and without the hint of a straw man) and the proceed to explain the faults in it. Of course, those he criticized cannot respond in the book but it did feel like a well humored fight.

This book was quite humbling as well. I recently read Why Buddhism Is True by Robert Wright and was very much convinced of the scientific “validation” of Buddhism (in fact, you can find a very generous review of Wright’s book on my GoodReads page). Not only has this book introduced me to problems people have with Buddhist modernism but it made me realized just how far from understanding the situation I was despite feeling as though I had a good grasp of it. I was previously convinced that I had to have been mostly on target seeing as “science” has “confirmed” these Buddhist ideas. Despite my efforts, I failed to notice scientific errors and philosophical errors in these findings.

Furthermore, if this short and simple book could so change my perspective so radically, surely any book could do the same. I only agree with all of Thompson’s finding being I heard out his entire explication. If Joseph Goldstein or the Dalai Lama wrote a book in response I am just as likely to change understandings again. If I am not careful and select a book by an author who is attempting to misguide (or are themselves misguided) then I could just as easily believe something untrue. I thought of myself as analytical, skeptical, and scientific but this book has prove that wrong. I think that is exactly who this book is for - those are the ones who are the most interested in neural Buddhism.

I highly recommend this book, it feels like the perfect bridge back to academics from the world of Buddhist modernism. If you are like me and recently went down the Buddhist rabbit hole, you might find this book to be a nice bookend.

title: Buddhism: One Teacher, Many Traditions
author: Dalai Lama XIV
review:
I enjoyed the book and felt like I got plenty out of it, I don’t know exactly who it’s for. If you are, like me, just curious about Buddhism then it is incredibly dense, dense with jargon, and doesn’t give a very in-depth understanding of anything specifically. If you are very familiar with Buddhism then I imagine you might be annoyed with the surface level explanations about common ideas bloating a book that’s suppose to talk about different traditions.

To clarify, this book is not a good introduction to Buddhism. If that’s what you’re looking for then look elsewhere (His Holiness has another book just for that). It’s also not a history of how the different traditions have changed and diverged over time - only a small section is focused on that. I felt like this book didn’t know exactly what it wanted to be. While I can only speculate, I believe they tried to write a book for everyone and ended up with a book for no one.

That said, I enjoyed learning about the different traditions. Simply reading about Buddhism allows me to hear how to properly use all the terms - and there are a lot of them. For that reason, unless you are incredibly familiar with Buddhism, I actually would suggest the audiobook over the physical book. I found my reading slowed to a halt as I tried to sound out the new terms.

title: The Social Leap: The New Evolutionary Science of Who We Are, Where We Come From, and What Makes Us Happy
author: William Von Hippel
review:
If you’re looking for a easy to read overview on evolutionary psychology, this is a break book to pick up! The sections the book is broken into each have their own clear purpose that doesn’t feel redundant (many nonfiction books have sections that make you wonder why they bothered naming them). I also was surprised by the great sense of humor the author has. Admittedly, he did go for the cheap jokes here and there and some felt shoe-horned in but I didn’t mind too much. It was almost charming - like a dad trying too hard to be funny but still getting laughs on the good jokes.

I picked this book up hoping to find a something about what evolution tells us about the way we act and was very pleased! It is concise, easy to read, and covers quite a bit of ground. If you have a similar itch, The Social Leap is a great way to scratch it without investing too much time or butting heads with a dense text. I also really appreciated the take always at the end of the book - it give actionable take always and, too a lesser extent, serves as a nice summary of each chapter.

title: Heidegger in 90 Minutes (Philosophers in 90 Minutes Series)
author: Paul Strathern
review:
Just discovered this series but I’m really enjoying it. This book is a wonderful overview of Heidegger and can serve as a great introduction to him. It give a brief history of his life, career, and major writings as well as some (arguably essential) historical context. Heidegger’s work can feel impenetrable so having a easy to read book like this to easy you into some of his ideas could be quite useful. How To Read Heidegger is another book that serves a similar purpose that might pair nicely with this one.

Beyond this books utility, it’s quite enjoyable. It is well written, easy to understand, and has a great sense of humor. I imagine I will be going through this series in the near future, learning about philosophers I’m less familiar with. I would also like to recommend the audiobook. It is short enough to get through in a day and if you listen while you get ready and travel you might not even have to set aside time for it. I’ve seen negative reviews of the narrator, Robert Whitfield, but I actually really enjoy his work. It can be a bit slow paced at time but nothing a quick playback speed adjustment can’t fixed.

title: Sartre in 90 Minutes (Philosophers in 90 Minutes Series)
author: Paul Strathern
review:
Quick and easy to read overview of Jean-Paul Sartre. For such a short book, it touches on quite a lot of his life and writings. Naturally, there is a lot left out but I would definitely recommend it to anyone who just wants a quick introduction to Sartre. If you are reading any of his book, it might be nice to give this a read to contextualize them a bit more. It also is a great survey of his work so if you just want to see what he has to off before jump into a longer book, this is a great option.

The end of the book also contains a couple of timelines that might be helpful. If you aren’t familiar with much western philosophy I’d actually recommend reading the philosophy timeline before reading the rest of the book. This particular-in 90 minutes book is free for audible subscribers. It’s read by Charlton Heston, who I though did a fantastic job. He reminds me of Richard Mathews, who I am definitely enjoy. Highly recommend this book to anyone interested in Sartre, existentialism, or philosophy around the time of WW2.

title: Deep Work: Rules for Focused Success in a Distracted World
author: Cal Newport
review:
There are a handful of genuinely useful advice in this book but I don’t think they made the journey worth it. So much of this book is the exact kind of productivity-guru banter that makes the self help genre hard to stomach at times. I actually though the book was very well written, easy to read, and the author sounds like a really great guy. I think I would love getting coffee and chatting with him. Some of the bold claim, over generalizations, and obsession with productively made it unenjoyable.

I don’t think everyone will have the same visceral response to this book that I did, if you can get through the introduction without feeling annoyed then I would highly recommend the book. I, however, found myself rolling my eyes more often than writing down notes. The paragraph at the beginning where he tries to convince you just how complicated SQL is felt almost condescending. The simplistic solutions like “just don’t use social media” felt idealistic. And, for reference, I am a graduate student studying computer science that does not use social media (unless you count GoodReads).

That said, I did leave with a couple of take always. Getting up early to get more done with no distractions is a great idea that I’ve been doing for awhile but this book helped me understand why I find this practice useful. I also enjoyed some of the ideas surrounding emails, specifically responding to filled out emails that close the loop as soon as possible. I wish I enjoyed the book more than I did, I sadly had to removed other Newport books from my reading list after this book.

title: Why Buddhism Is True: The Science and Philosophy of Meditation and Enlightenment
author: Robert  Wright
review:
Misleading and less than scientific. I originally loved this book after reading but after further research I discovered how fault many of its premises are and how unscientific many of the claims are. In attempting to combine Buddhism and science, it misses most of what make Buddhism Buddhism and fails to understand science. The book is focused on evolutionary psychology, which is deemed a pseudo-science and falls short at a expressing what Buddhism is. As Evan Thompson put it in Why I Am Not Buddhist, where he critics this book in particular, saying science supports Buddhism is like saying science supports art. In fact, science has nothing to say about art and art has nothing to say about science, that’s simply not what either do. A book title “Why Christianity is True” that tries to use science to justify a few moral lessons from Christianity would not sell as well. It seems, however, that with a religion less understood by western readers, it is easier to not notice the flaws, as I did not when I was reading this book.

I dropped my review from 4 stars to 3 stars - I can’t deny I really enjoy reading this book but don’t feel comfortable giving it as positive as a rating now. This book did introduce me to Buddhist ideas that have become more important to me but the misleading nature of it makes it hard to recommend. If you are set on reading this, just promise yourself that you will read Why I Am Not A Buddhist afterwards and do some research on the criticisms of evolutionary psychology. If you’re not so set, I highly recommend reading Advice Not Give by Mark Epstein. He doesn’t go into the science of Buddhism (which is a bit of an oxymoron anyway) but he does discuss science along with Buddhist teaching that are less misguided and more practical.

Below is my unedited original review I wrote just after reading Why Buddhism Is True. I still respect the author and am very excited to see more from him in the future.

——————

Original review: Effectively, this book is an introduction to a western interpretation of Buddhist teachings. As such, you get a high level overview of some teachings the western and secular world has found insightful from Buddhist ideas. You also get short descriptions of modern theories and studies that Wright claims supports these Buddhist teachings. Mixed in you will also so find anecdotes of the author’s experience learning about meditation and beginning to practice it.

I wasn’t sure what I was getting going into this book but I’m pretty happy with what I found. It’s basically a behavioral psychology book that references a western Buddhist ideology. I thought that gave the book a really nice flavor to it, some behavioral psychology books can come across as a bit dry. Additionally, I loved the through line of the book about the Robert Wright journey through meditation. Having a thin narrative through nonfiction is always welcome.

Not long after reading this books I was told by a someone who studies Buddhist philosophy to drop it. Before you read this, you should be aware that it is a bit of a controversial book. It exemplifies the often criticized “Buddhist Modernism” or “Neuro Buddhism” by taking an overly western interpretation of Buddhist ideas. While I can’t say I fully understand the criticism, it is something readers might want to be aware of.

Overall, I really enjoyed this book. It was fun, interesting, and very insightful. It opened me up to new curiosities - by the time I was half way through I had added multiple evolutionary psychology books to my reading list and started reading a book on the varieties of Buddhist practices. I genuinely recommend this book to anyone interested western Buddhism or behavioral psychology.

title: A Short History of Nearly Everything
author: Bill Bryson
review:
If you’re a fan of Cosmos, be it the book or any of the shows, you’ll love this book. It is actually incredibly similar to the Cosmos book - it is an overview of the history of science. This book, however, is surprisingly funny. As much as I love Sagan’s Cosmos show, the book can be a bit too dry. A Short History of Nearly everything has an incredible sense of humor. The author also breaks the forth wall at times, talking about his conversations with experts he had while researching the book.

It is quite extraordinary and humbling to hear the history of all human knowledge. It clear the author share a similar love of humanity and science as Sagan himself. By learn how much human’s know about the world we live in, you pay more attention to how little be know. And yet, as put in the last chapter, we are the only ones who can know. The information is well presented and well put together. I highly recommend this book.

title: Tribe: On Homecoming and Belonging
author: Sebastian Junger
review:
