While not exactly what I was hoping for going into this book, I still enjoyed it. The book is stories of war experience mixed with psychology - all under the theme of being a member of a “tribe” and evolution. If that sounds interesting, you should pick it up. The book is very short, you could plow through it in a day if you wanted, but I genuinely think it changed my understanding of communities.

Additionally, the way the book is written is very skin-able. It is a lot of two paragraph anecdotes, stories, and case studies. If you’re not interest in the overly detailed experience (which doesn’t always change the impact of the point) it’s quite easy to skim past it and not have to back track to figure out what’s going on. I wanted to give it three starts but the fact that it’s so concise and had a real impact on my world view forced me to bump it up to at least 4 stars. If I was more interested in war I might have given it 5.

title: Atomic Habits: An Easy & Proven Way to Build Good Habits & Break Bad Ones
author: James Clear
review:
Fun light read about how habits can have an impact and ways to improve habits in simple but effective ways. Anyone who’s payed attention to their habits have probably come across many of his tips but even so it can be useful to hear them explained clearly and concisely. The book is pretty straight forward, each chapter is basically a lesson and each lesson falls under one of his high rules of thumb. The advice is something I think most people should have at least a simple understanding of so I definitely would recommend reading it.

The author become well known in the world of habits manly from his blog and it definitely shows in the text. Each chapter is very formulaic - I can easily see how these could have been past blog posts. Each chapter starts with an anecdote then leads that into a way to improve habits and ends with a clear explanation of how to apply the rule. That’s the book. If that sounds enjoyable then you’ll love the book, if it sounds boring you probably won’t love it. I happened to enjoy that formal and think it will make individual chapters easy to revisit in the future.

title: Getting Things Done: The Art of Stress-Free Productivity
author: David    Allen
review:
If you are considering reading this, buy a used copy and just ready chapters 4-8. If you’re curious or feel lost, go back and read 1-4 and if you’re really invested in David Alan and the GTD methodology then finish the rest of the book. Chapters 4-8 (and even 4 is questionable) have some amazing and thoughtful insight into an interesting and useful methodology.

Getting the methodology out of this book isn’t ideal but it is worth the effort. The book just isn’t captivating to say the least and a lot of it is unnecessary for understanding the system. If you’re interested in getting more organized and implementing a system to manage the things you need to do, GTD is the nuclear option. You will spend a week or more getting it set up but it definitely will be worth it.

I’m giving the book 3 stars because it’s clear Alan has a great system but his writing skills are less clear. You can get a lot out of just watching an interview with him (Simplify is a podcast by Blinkist, I’d recommend either of their two interviews with him). But I definitely recommend the book still, just be aware of what you’re getting yourself into.

title: Why We Sleep: Unlocking the Power of Sleep and Dreams
author: Matthew Walker
review:
Uses intentionally misleading statistics and references low quality studies. I loved this book when I read it but after some digging it appears Dr. Walker was less than honest while writing it. The lessons are still great and much of the facts are solid but a surprising amount are not. He has been criticized by many scholars and researchers in his field, claiming he was spreading bad information with the book. As much as I love these pop-science nonfiction books, there are some that aren’t perfectly honest and this appears to be one of them. I dropped my original 4 star review to 3 stars. I think it’s still fine to read but take the statistics and studies with a grain of salt and if one speaks to you then take the time to look into it. Also, don’t stress too much about your sleep as a lot of the misleading facts are skewed to make you more worried than you should be.

Here is my original review from right after I read Why We Sleep for the first time. I still think it’s a decent book, just a bit misleading.

——————
Original review: A more descriptive title might be “The Importance of Sleep,” if the book still interested you with that title, I highly recommend it. There are some earlier chapters about “why we sleep” but the resounding answer is “because we do” and that we don’t fully understand why. The majority of the book is about studies that help us understand the effect that sleep has on us. While the text was a bit dry at times, it did it’s job wonderfully and was far more interesting than I anticipated.

While I have not read many books on sleep, I believe this one is an incredible overview of it and how it effects us. It has convinced me of the incredible importance of sleep and, as such, I can’t help but recommend it to everyone. Sleep, according to Dr. Walker, is as critical (or more, in a way) than diet and physical activity in one’s health. I wouldn’t just recommend this book, I believe it is critical that most people read it. Despite how important sleep is, we are horribly uneducated about it and our western culture has destructive idea surrounding it that should be avoided.

This sounds dramatic but anyone who values there health and happiness should read this book. I knew sleep was important and that I should be more mindful of it but Why We Sleep has helped me understand not only how to improve my sleep but also why I must.

title: Phenomenology (The MIT Press Essential Knowledge series)
author: Chad Engelland
review:
Great high level introduction to phenomenology. Multiple chapters were very confusing to read but I have the impression that’s more of a problem with the subject and not the way it was presented. Quite reassuringly, Engelland talks about the stages of becoming a phenomenologist and the first stage involves just figuring out it’s language. I wish this section came in earlier but it was nice to have it there to remind me it’s okay to not understand it on my first read.

Each chapter can more or less be read on its own, I might have enjoyed more of a through line but I think this format will make the book easier to return to. Given its form factor, I think that was intentional - it is almost meant to be a coffee table book. I would definitely recommend it to anyone interested in phenomenology or philosophy of the last century. It’s a great overview that talks about context you might not find in other books.

title: Going to Pieces without Falling Apart: A Buddhist Perspective on Wholeness
author: Mark Epstein
review:
Interesting combination of psychotherapy and Buddhism. Epstein does a great job at presenting his Buddhist beliefs the way he might to a patient. As someone who is not religious, I found his Buddhist antidotes to be very insightful. There is not much structure to the book, it is a sort of free form flow of thoughts and personal examples. While I might have enjoyed more of a through line, the ill-structure form made it easy to casual pick up and put back down. It’s a very short read (~180 pages with generous spacing between lines) so you don’t have much to lose by picking it up.

Before this book, I read Mark Epstein’s more recent book, Advice Not Given. If you’ve read that, they are incredibly similar. The both serve their own purpose but follow a nearly identical format. If you have not read Advice Not Given, I think I prefer that book so you might want to look at that one instead. They’re both enjoyable and informative reads but I don’t know if it’s necessary to read both. However, I’d you’re developing an interesting in Buddhism, then these book are an incredible introduction grounded for the western reader in western ideals.

title: Advice Not Given: A Guide to Getting Over Yourself
author: Mark Epstein
review:
Fun, loosely structured, book about meditation, therapy, and Buddhism. I wasn’t sure what the book was “about” at first, it’s rambling of anecdotes and turning points for the author and people he knows. I mean that in the best way possible, it feels very fun and casual. I avoided the book for a while thinking the Buddhist references wouldn’t be fun but I actually found them incredibly useful and memorable.

Basically, the book is broken up into eight parts - each a step of the Buddhist eight fold path. Each of which is a principle to guide action an behavior to help you reach “enlightenment.” I use quotations there because, in this book, it’s less about any religion enlightenment and more about just being happy. In each step, Epstein explains the meaning and provides stories of it being implemented (sometimes well, sometimes poorly).

I’m surprised I enjoyed it as much as I did, I definitely would recommend this book to anyone interested in mindfulness and meditation. Further, I would especially recommend it to people who, like me, have no interest in anything religious. The way he introduces Buddhism was very interesting and he never strayed away from the practical advice of it that loses nothing in a secular context.

title: Meditation for Fidgety Skeptics: A 10% Happier How-To Book
author: Dan   Harris
review:
Entertaining writing with useful information, a perfect follow up to 10% happier. If you’ve read 10% Happier and are sold on meditation but need help getting into it, this is a must read. If, on the other hand, you’re not sold or otherwise disinterested in meditation, it’s probably not for you.

It’s easy to write a dry “how to” book that’s useful but not enjoyable but this book is a bit of both. It can be hard to figure out what this book is exactly about but there is a pretty clear narrative once you’ve read it. Dan Harris got together with like minded friends, rented a tour bus, and went across the country asking people who want to meditate but aren’t why they haven’t gotten into the habit yet. The book is the story of that road trip with guided meditations, personal anecdotes, and insights they learned from the road trip mixed in.

Along with the loose narrative, you also get to see the relationship between the two coauthors grow and develop as the book goes on. What one wrote is clearly distinguished from the other so a lot of the book feels like a conversation. Both have a great since of humor that are very similar to one another. You’ll have fun reading it and come out with a lot of insight into meditation.

title: 10% Happier
author: Dan   Harris
review:
Dan Harris presents, in this book, a wonderful introduction to the world meditation by letting you look through his eyes as he discovered it himself. To put it concisely, I highly recommend this book as a gateway into meditation and mindfulness. It doesn’t take itself too seriously, it doesn’t promise you a life altering experience, and it leaves out the pseudo-science.

As someone who did not meditate before reading this book but was mostly sold on the idea based on recent research suggesting real world benefits, it was the tipping point. Not to claim it’s a world changing read but it brought me from “I know I should meditate, I just don’t” to “yeah, I guess I should get on that.” Dan Harris, in his quest to understand mindfulness, always seemed to ask similar questions that I had and usually he found pretty satisfying answers. This may just be a generational difference but I did find his assumption that most people thought of meditation as pan-flute-y poppycock a little annoying. Every opportunity he had to say how skeptical he was of it, he doubled and tripled down. It by no means ruined anything, however. Hopefully it did what I think he was attending to do and won over the more uncertain readers.

I couldn’t get enough of his writing style, it is goofy and engaging even when talking about more complicated topics (which he doesn’t really get into much). Dan Harris writes like a genuinely funny youth pastor. I mean that in the best possible way. His jokes are always just safe enough to not bother anyone but with the hint of an edge. For example, he sure does love talking about how his wife thinks he’s a jerk. Another fun quark is his new anchor sentence structure. You can hear the period coming from the first word of the sentence. It might be grating to some readers but for me it made the book a lot more fun.

Fantastic read, if you think meditation is probably something you should consider and you want a book to read, pick this one up. By that, I mean this can easily be your “just for fun, right before bed” book and not you “learn about meditation” book. Maybe you’ll pick up a useful habit after reading or maybe you’ll just get some context for the video of that news anchor having a panic attack on air. Either way, you’ll probably be happy you read it.

title: At the Existentialist Café
author: Sarah Bakewell
review:
Absolutely loved reading this book; those interested in existentialism, 20th century history, and modern philosophy will get a lot out of it. While the structure isn’t what you’d expect, it’s not quite as linear as you might assume a history book is, there are no slow points and the writer does a wonderful job at flowing ideas together seamlessly.

There’s a surprising amount going on in this book. It could easily have been a well put together summation of the history of existentialism and I would have been perfectly pleased. However, the author presents the philosophers and events as the characters they are, not merely names on a book. She also intertwines her personal connection to existentialism very eloquently. At the beginning she talks about how she discovered it (at that point, the reader will probably be at a similar point) and at the end she talks about the journey she had been on as she wrote the book (again, mirroring the readers journey having just read it).

I could go on about the structure and presentation but I will resist the urge. Know that it is a pleasure to read and very informative. I will be rereading this book within the next year.

title: Yes to Life: In Spite of Everything
author: Viktor E. Frankl
review:
First off, three stars is still a positive review, I just was not impacted much by this book. It is a series of take Frankl gave after WW2, all connected and some better than others. It is very apparent from the writing style that these are speeches given in front of a crowd - some readers may find this an enjoyable style but I did not. I don’t fault anybody for this, it’s just the nature of this type of text (although it’s not always the case).

The writing style left me unsatisfied but the content did not. Frankl talks about his time in concentration camps, his search for meaning, and the struggles others face with meaning. Some of his stories will certainly stick with me for years to come.

I do, however, have to wonder, why does this book exist? Not the original writing or speeches but the 2020 English translation. The content struggles to fill a book; some of the added texts from other authors feels redundant, the margins are comedically large, and I doubt there will ever be a paper back edition seeing as the hardback fills slim as is. More importantly, however, I don’t know it’s audience. For its original release, I have no question but for this recently English copy, who is it for? Readers who are familiar with the amazing book Man’s Search For Meaning and will have heard most of these stories, told better even. Those who have somehow found Say Yes To Life but not Man’s Search For Meaning will feel too little content is provided to flesh out the context. It’s hard to casually mentioned the author narrowly survived a concentration camp.

I don’t mean to say this is a bad book but with the existence of Man’s Search For Meaning, I don’t know how I could recommend it. If you haven’t read Man’s Search For Meaning, read that instead. If you have read Man’s Search For Meaning, you will gain more from rereading it than picking up Yes To Life. If you have read the former book dozens of times and just want more Frankl content then, and only then, I can recommend you read Say Yes To Life.

title: How to Read Heidegger
author: Mark A. Wrathall
review:
Informative, enjoyable, but not fully what title implies.

As much as I enjoyed reading this book and as great of an overview of Heidegger it is, I can’t recommend it as a guide for reading him. It presents several passages written by Heidegger and then explains them, quite well I should add. However, it doesn’t leave you with any insight on how to go about reading him. The book was focused on “but this Heidegger means...” instead of “You’ll notice with Heidegger, he often...” As enjoyable and enlightening as the explanation is, you will not be any less lost with the different passage from the same author.

Ideally the book would have given tips and explained Heidegger’s writing style but it did not. Based on the title I had hoped for a book that would tell me how he often took nouns and used them as verbs, how to interpret that when you encounter it, etc. Instead it was a straightforward explanation of what you just read.

I’m still giving it four stars because it is well written and enjoyable. The title felt a bit misleading to me is all. If you are new to Heidegger though, it goes from his famous Being and Time into his later years, giving a nice overview of his path. It also provides context when needed which can fill you in on his life as well. It’s a short read but worth it if you’re interested in the subject.

title: Husserl’s Phenomenology
author: Dan Zahavi
review:
Clear and concise explication of Husserl’s philosophy as well as some useful context. At 144 pages (of content that is, excluding index, etc.), it serves as a wonderful introduction to phenomenology. I am not well versed in his work so I can’t speak to its faithfulness but I have heard those more acquainted with his writing praise it highly for its well rounded yet short explanation. The author makes it clear when he is injecting his own opinion and at the end he directly explains what what he left out and further context of Husserl’s work as a whole.

As clear as the book is, I would recommend reading it with a highlighter in hand. It is dense insofar as it throws a lot of jargon at you at once. However, the author does a wonderful job of breaking those explications up with contextual paragraphs. He also is not shy about repeating himself for the sake of clarity. There are many “To reiterate...” and “To summarize...” riddled throughout the book, each of which very welcomed.

This is not a good book for someone with no background in philosophy but is not impenetrable for them. Ideally you will have a basic background of Aristotle, Descartes, Kant, etc. but you could probably get away with just looking up terms as you go. That said, you do not have to be an expert to read it, it is very clear and in very plain English. Definitely recommend it for anyone interested in phenomenology.

title: Existentialism is a Humanism
author: Jean-Paul Sartre
review:
Quick and insightful read, a must for anyone interested in existentialism. I don’t know that I would recommend it as an entry point, however. Sartre is speaking to a crowd that is familiar with his work and works of others in his field. I found myself looking up names and words as I read to fill in the gaps.

Despite the title, this book is comprised of much more than Sartre’s talk under the same name. It includes a very brief question and answer section from the audience. I found is enjoyable to read the audience’s discussion on it, it made the book feel more alive and less one sided. I will, however, say I started to get lost when the contemporary writer stepped in to critique Sartre. It also includes a preface that adds context to the speech, which I found very interesting and helpful and, more notably, it includes his analysis of Albert Camus’ The Stranger. Anyone who is familiar with that work owes it to themselves to read Sartre’s incredible analysis of it, I came out of it feeling like I understood the book and Camus’ philosophy much more clearly.

This was a very enjoyable and easy read, absent of the dense and confusing prose often associated with Sartre. I will certainly be reading the speech again but may skip out on the rest upon a second reading.

title: Thus Spoke Zarathustra
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
review:
This book is certainly for everyone and no one; to put it concisely, it is at time an enjoyable read with thought provoking ideas and at others it defies understanding entirely. I can’t tell if the latter makes it a more interesting read or a more frustrating one, perhaps both.

Full disclosure, I read the Barnes & Noble edition (which has a lovely introduction) and only read it once. While graduate students will continue to write their thesis on a single page from this book for years to come, I will be discussing it as it was to me - a book. But beware, that is possibly the worst way to read it, I will definitely read it again one day and get much more out of it.

As a casual reader, I really enjoyed the quasi-narrative presented (heaviest in the prelude and book four). It was an entertaining biblical parody that seemed, to me, to walk the like of making fun of the Christian bible and paying tribute to it. Not that it glorifies Christianity in anyway, it just seemed to take full advantage of a similar format and it’s most important document.

Other parts, I really had to forces myself through. I don’t think it was poor writing decisions that made it this way but I don’t dismiss that theory either. It is incredibly difficult to understand, like attempting to speed read Shakespeare as a twenty first-century American. There is since in the words but you have to search for it. The oddest part, however, is how quick it reads. There are few German words, obscure references, or over the top language to slow you down. It is just confusingly written.

If you’re curious about this book, go ahead and read it. It is a genuinely enjoyable read even when the reading isn’t helping you understand the text. Some of the poetry is truly moving and some the passages are mostly intelligible.

title: The Future of Humanity: Terraforming Mars, Interstellar Travel, Immortality and Our Destiny Beyond Earth
author: Michio Kaku
review:
Very fun book to scratch that science channel itch. It’s a enjoyable survey of science and astronomy with a hint of a narrative (that being the narrative of the human race). Think an Issac Asimov book but instead of telling a story he tells you a series of potential stories.

Towards the beginning it almost feels like an episode of Cosmos, explains simple scientific concepts that you may not know. That never really goes away but the deep into the book you go, the more it becomes about contemplating the, well, future of humanity. Towards the end it get pretty crazy as he predicts the end of the universe and it is equally inspiring and haunting.

Recommend this as a fun casual read for anyone who grew up watching the science channel and reading sci-fi but never went into the field. Definitely suitable for young readers as well, I can’t imagine how many times I would have re-read this as a kid.

title: I'm Thinking of Ending Things
author: Iain Reid
review:
This book is a good, short read, that begs to be read a second time. The story is interesting but the dialogue and narration is what really carries the book.

The writing style is very simplistic and direct - maying it an easy and fast read - which is in addition to the already a short size at 200 pages with incredibly generous text spacing. I think this is a positive for this book, a nearly all dialogue book could easily outstay its welcome and this book avoids that. It also encourages a second reading which is almost necessary to get the full effect of the book.

I won’t spoil anything but the themes and ideas in the book are very thought provoking, even when they aren’t perfectly executed. I highly recommend this book for anyone who enjoys idea driven books with a mystery.

For anyone considering this book in relation to the Charlie Kaufman film adaptation; one will spoil the twist for the other but you can appreciate both on their own despite that. Is recommended the movie first, as preferred it (but note that they go for very different things), and then reading the book to add context. Both are great though and don’t need to be though of in relation to the other.

title: The Myth of Sisyphus
author: Albert Camus
review:
A pillar of existential philosophy, Camus’ The Myth of Sisyphus is an enlightening read that left me equal parts understood and unfulfilled (but to no fault of the text).

If you’re considering this book but are worried it is too dense, don’t be too put off by it. It is very manageable for an average reader but require a little more attention. Don’t hesitate to reread pages or look up occasionally references - I’d you take your time you will be paid off for it.

I highly recommend this book to everyone but I think it is best discovered instead of recommended. If the ideas of Camus speak to you then pick this book up but don’t force yourself to if they do not. For me, however, I will think of it often and be revisiting it in the near future.

title: The Art of Living: The Classical Manual on Virtue, Happiness and Effectiveness
author: Epictetus
review:
This book is a modern interpretation of Epictetus’ Stoicism by someone with no scholarly experience with philosophy - I think Epictetus would be quite proud of this fact.

Effectively, this is a self help book filled with short blurbs about how you should live. It just so happens that the advice was thought of a couple thousand years ago. The writing is very clear and concise (in the mordant interpretation anyway, the short essays, though enjoyable, were not so concise). It was very enjoyable to read and the points are incredibly insightful.

I’m not the first to point this out but I do find some of the inconsistencies in logic to be a little jarring in a couple of places but it was mostly coherent. Some of the ideas have not aged quite as well as others but I found these more charming than distracting.

It is clear this book just nearly justified being in a printed book - there are pages with just two sentences on them, there are some short essays that some might consider filler, and the margins are unusually large despite the already small form factor of the book. Just know, going into it, this is a very quick read but I actually appreciated that. It give you more time to chew on the information and encourages re-readings.

I highly recommend this book, while it isn’t perfect it is insightful and very quick to read. It won’t take you a full day to read so maybe pick it up between two other books or for your next flight. The information will leave you questioning your actions and looking for ways you can improve yourself and your happiness.

title: A History of Western Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell
review:
This book is very dry and very long but has a lot going for it. It is very much a history book but the author injects his own philosophical opinions and assessments as you travel through time. While is is divided up by philosophers and movements, it reads like a narrative (which history is).

Again, Russell’s writing is incredibly dry but it has its own quarks I came to love. He, for example, has little interest in praising philosophers unless they have contributed something very important, in his mind. At multiple points he simply said “but this person is not important.” It was also fun to see him poke and prod at philosophers I have never heard others speak ill of.

One of my favorite aspects of his writing is his very subtle, very British, sense of humor. If you are not paying attention you may not even notice how many jokes he put in the book but they are very welcome. One of my favorites is, and I quote,

“... Nietzsche’s Superman is very like Siegfried, except that he knows Greek. This may seem odd, but that is not my fault.”

That is the closest to a direct joke I found in the book.

Anyone interested in philosophy or the history of human knowledge should have this book on their shelf. Just know you may decide to not read it in one go as the author intended. Instead, you might just use it as reference for when you want to read up on a section of history. If you do read it in one go, as I did, don’t feel too bad for skimming or even skipping a chapter here and there. The text can be slow to read during the most interesting parts so by the time you get to something that doesn’t interest you (or the writer directly states that it is not very important) then you may decide it does require your full attention.

title: Astrophysics for People in a Hurry
author: Neil deGrasse Tyson
review:
Very fast read that will be worth going back too. Neil deGrasse Tyson does a great job at putting his own sense of humor into a very science heavy book - but be warned, that might be a bad thing for some. He humor exemplifies 2010 popular “geek” humor. I found the way it has aged poorly to be as entertaining as the joke would have been otherwise so it was a net gain for me.

The information, however, is wonderful. It was very insightful, albeit hard to keep up with at times. I recently rewatched his original Cosmos series and found they paired incredibly well. If you’re a fan of that series, you’ll love this book.

title: The Forgetting Machine: Memory, Perception, and the "Jennifer Aniston Neuron"
author: Rodrigo Quian Quiroga
review:
Pretty enjoyable and informative read. It did not go as into the philosophy of the topic as I expected - confusing mainly on the psychology and neuroscience side of it - but I don’t hold that against it, it might however make me bias against the book a bit. The writing was adequate, nothing to exciting but nothing too dry. Overall I’m glad I read it but don’t feel the need to recommend it to anyone who is not already interested.

That said, three stars is still a positive review. I don’t think the content will stick with me too much (sans a couple of case studies) or drastically change my perspective on much. If you want to learn more about memory in broad strokes this book isn’t a bad introduction. While fairly different in content, I would recommend Thinking, Fast and Slow before you get to this one.

title: Nausea
author: Jean-Paul Sartre
review:
The unique premise of this book being a found journal is engaging it never felt gimmicky. Having the book be composed of journal entries means Sartre was free to spend pages just discussing ideas and not being to concerned with the actual story (but at no point was the story forgotten). Sometimes you would run into a day’s entry that was only a few words long and you can’t help but wonder what must have happened that day.

Once you get past the format, the loose narrative and heavy ideas are highly engaging. The book is mostly about our main character’s thoughts as he comes to a couple of realizations that are somehow independent but highly intertwined. As a reader, you get to be a part of this journey, almost playing detective and arm chair psychologist, watching and considering where the writer is headed. Meanwhile the ideas presented are very enlightening, I often say the book down to do some journaling of my own.

That back of the book hardly tells you why you will be reading but I hope that you take a leap of faith and read anyway. It only improves the “found journal” appeal of the book.

title: Man's Search for Meaning
author: Viktor E. Frankl
review:
I regret giving any other book five stars because I cannot give Man’s Search For Meaning anymore. To put it lightly, it is an life changing read that touches on philosophy, psychology, history, sociology, religion, and more all on one relatively short package.

There’s isn’t anything I can say that hasn’t been said a thousand time before. I will, however, speak to the edition I read. My copy is the from 2014 by Beacon Press - it is a very well structured book that adds supplemental reading to the original. It builds up the context and importance with a forward, has a similar afterword, and concludes with a series of speeches and letters Frankl wrote. I highly recommend this printing but I am sure every other one is incredible as well.

title: A Happy Death
author: Albert Camus
review:
This book pairs nicely with The Stranger; it is very clearly Camus’ first attempt to write The Strange but it also a completely different book. I felt Camus’ voice more intertwined with our protagonist and to some extent that made him more relatable. It is a slightly more stranger read (no pun intended) because of the less indirect storyline and slightly confusing timeline. Besides that it was a wonderful read that left me with a better understanding of Camus’ take on living and death.

I give it four stars only because I gave The Stranger five and enjoyed this book a bit less. If there was a half star rest assured this would be a four and a half star rating.

title: Money: The True Story of a Made-Up Thing
author: Jacob Goldstein
review:
Very insightful book about the concept and history of money. It reads like a narrative, starting at the very start of money and ends on what the future of money entail. In between you’ll find clear and well written antidotes about its evolution. If you have no interest in money or economics, this is still an incredible read.

There is a lot in this book that can be directly applied to modern day money. It will give you insights into why our current system is the way it is, how it is reminiscent of past systems, and (most importantly) why there was legal tender US dollars with pictures of Santa on them. At the onset of the book, I found the way the author uses of the word “money” odd but now I can’t help but use it in a similar way.

I’ve only spoken well of this book but gave it 4 stars; it’s nothing the book did wrong, it just didn’t have a fundamental impact on me that some other books have. While it has changed the way I think about money, I don’t think it will change much in my day-to-day life.

title: Understanding Exposure: How to Shoot Great Photographs with a Film or Digital Camera
author: Bryan Peterson
review: Incredibly effective and intuitive guide on exposure. You will come out of it with a solid foundation of photography. If you read it, I know it can be tempting to skip the captions on the pictures but I promise it is one of the most useful parts. Highly recommend this book for anyone getting into photography.

title: The Stranger
author: Albert Camus
review: The tone of the narrator felt so unsettling yet somehow comforting. From the narration alone I slowly became more content with my place in the world. It was a memorable read in the first half but by the second half (particularly towards the end) the book became something I will never forget. It reminded me what’s important and why I should be happy with where I am. It may comes across as morbid but it is a surprisingly uplifting story.
